Party Ideas & Guides

Party Games for 5 Year Olds: What Actually Works at an Aussie Party

The party games for 5 year olds that actually work are short, fast moving and designed so no child ends up on the sidelines. I plan ten to fifteen minutes for each one, keep the rules to a single sentence, and leave out anything that knocks children out one by one.

Why elimination games fail Six games that work Prizes without the tears

That is most of the formula right there. If you would rather browse a ready made list first, there are plenty of party games that suit a five year old to choose between for indoor and backyard parties. Below is what changes at this age, the games I come back to again and again, and how to hold the energy steady from the first knock at the door to the last goodbye.

What is different about turning five

Five is a lovely age to plan for, but it is a narrow target. Most children at a fifth birthday stay with one activity for ten to fifteen minutes before looking around for the next thing. They are not bored, they are simply done.

Physical ability is all over the place too. In one group you will have a child who can skip, hop and balance on one foot, and another still working out how to run and change direction without ending up on the grass. Games that reward the fastest child always deliver the same winner, and the others work that out quickly.

Reading is the other thing people forget. Many five year olds know their own name and a handful of words, so anything built on written clues or scorekeeping will stall. Pictures and colours do the same job without the frustration. Feelings matter as well, because losing is genuinely upsetting at five, and one upset child can tip the whole room.

Why I leave elimination games out

This is the single biggest change I would make to a standard party games list. The traditional versions of musical chairs, dodgeball and most tag games remove children one at a time, so the child who goes out first spends the longest stretch of the party doing nothing. That child is usually the youngest or least confident, and the one most likely to melt down or ask to go home.

Every classic game has a version that keeps everybody in:

Non elimination versions of classic party games for five year olds
The classic versionThe version that keeps everybody in
Musical chairsMusical cushions, where children share as the cushions disappear and everyone cheers when five of them squeeze onto one
TagA tagged child freezes until a friend crawls under their arm to free them
DodgeballA target game where each child throws at a stack of cups in turn

The effect is easy to see on the day. Nobody is counting who is out, nobody argues about whether they were really tagged, and you are not managing disappointed guests on the edge of the lawn. If running all of this while also handling food, photos and a dozen parents sounds like a lot, entertainers who run the games for you take that job off your hands so you can simply be there for your child.

Games that work at a fifth birthday

Freeze dance and musical statues

Put music on, let them dance, pause the track and everyone holds still. Instead of calling children out, I give the wobbliest statue a silly job, such as pressing pause on the next round. Two minutes of setup, no equipment, and it works on a deck or in a lounge room.

What's the Time Mr Wolf

One child stands with their back to the group as Mr Wolf, the others call out the question, and they creep forward by the number of steps given. When Mr Wolf calls dinner time, everyone runs back to the start line. It suits a long backyard or a hallway, and the role can rotate so lots of children get a turn.

Simon Says

A quiet winner for the stretch just before or after food, because it needs no running and no gear. Keep the instructions physical and funny rather than tricky, because the joy at five is in the wobbling and giggling, not in catching anybody out.

Duck Duck Goose

A circle game that is easy to explain and easy to rejoin. The chase is short, turns come around fast, and children who are not keen on running still sit in the circle and feel part of it.

A picture card scavenger hunt

Rather than written clues, I print or draw simple pictures of things to find, such as a leaf, something red or a hat. Children work in pairs with an adult walking behind. It fills fifteen minutes and gives the fast movers somewhere to put all that energy.

Pin the thing on the thing

Match it to the theme rather than buying something generic, so pin the tail on the unicorn, the fin on the shark or the spot on the ladybird. A blindfold makes some five year olds anxious, so offer the option of closing their eyes instead.

How long to run each game, and when to move on

I write a loose order of events rather than a timetable, because no plan survives a group of five year olds. Arrival and free play, two active games, food, a calm game, the main event, then a wind down. Each block sits at roughly ten to fifteen minutes, which gives you five or six slots across a two hour party and a couple of spares in reserve.

The signal to move on is not the clock, it is the group. When three or four children drift towards the trampoline or the toy box, that game is finished no matter how much time you allocated. Having the next thing ready to start is what keeps the party from going sideways. Quiet activities are the other half of it, because five year olds cannot run for two hours straight, and face painting keeps a queue of children happy for a decent stretch while the rest of the group keeps playing.

Indoors, outdoors and a plan for the weather

December and January parties here are usually outdoor parties, which is great for noise and mess but demands some thought. The hottest part of the day is worth avoiding, so a morning or late afternoon start is kinder on everybody. Shade, water bottles and somewhere to sit matter more than any game on your list, and hats and sunscreen at the door save fuss later.

A few things worth doing before the first guest arrives:

  • Walk the yard. Clear sticks, sprinkler heads and anything else waiting to trip a running child.
  • Skip the sprinting games on hard surfaces. Save those for grass.
  • Write a second list. Pick three games that work in a cleared lounge room or garage, and know where the furniture is going.

That way you are not inventing a wet weather plan at nine in the morning while it rains.

Prizes without the tears

Participation prizes are the easiest fix for the competitive side of party games. Something tiny for every child who joins in, handed out at the end of each game rather than to a single winner, takes the sting out of losing.

Where you do want a winner, rotate the type of challenge so different children get their moment, because a guessing game, a throwing game and a silly game spread the wins far better than three running races. Keep the prizes identical, since five year olds notice a difference in colour or size instantly.

Frequently asked questions

How do I make a birthday special for a 5 year old?

Build the day around what your child is into right now, and let them choose two or three things themselves, such as the theme, one game and what goes on the table. Five year olds remember being the centre of attention more than they remember the decorations, so a crown, a seat of honour and their favourite songs go a long way.

How do I keep kids entertained at a party?

Change activity every ten to fifteen minutes and always have the next thing ready to start. Alternate loud and active games with quiet seated ones so the group does not hit exhaustion too early, and keep a couple of spare games in reserve for when the schedule slips.

What can you play with 5 people at home?

Small groups suit circle and turn taking games, so Simon Says, Duck Duck Goose, freeze dance and a picture card treasure hunt all work with five children. With a group that size you can also run a craft activity properly, because everybody sits at one table and gets help when they need it.
